chapter: Rockwell: playing with the Lewis band
title: Playing banjo with the George Lewis band
summary: Rockwell calls the rhythm section the greatest musical experience of his life, and says Lewis gave no instructions.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: How did playing with the George Lewis band compare with any other bands you have played with, Dr. Rockwell?

Well, the rhythm section, I would say it was probably the greatest musical experience of my life, even probably to this time, at least on banjo. I remember the third or fourth number was Chinatown, and the tempo was the only time in my life I've never been able to keep up on a 4-4 tempo, because it was... It was a little faster than that. And I remember looking around, and drag was keeping up, and I kept it up for two choruses, and I thought I was going to have a heart attack, and I went, you know, and these guys were old, and their temples were quite fast, although once you got used to it, then you could kind of keep up, you know,
once you got kind of wound up.

Yeah. The rhythm section was super solid and swinging, and I used to put Alton Purnell down. I didn't like his style at all, and when I played with him, I realized that he was a swinging piano player, you know. When I was a listener, I didn't think he was that good, but when I played, I saw how important he was in the band. The whole... everybody in the rhythm section was excellent.
Was this... this was about Howard and Robinson were playing with the band?
No, Howard and Robinson were playing. They were playing?
Oh, yeah. That's what I thought. Well, now, when you played with them, did George Lewis give you any special instructions or advice?
Nobody hardly would tell me the key or anything. You just had to make it. They would just go... they'd kick it off and that's it.
You hardly even know what it was on the world. That's right. But he didn't tell you anything about, like, okay, play four four, play this or do that or...?

No, I knew what he wanted because I knew... I knew Moreiro's style, you know, and I couldn't take the Trevelo's chorus that he would do on Closer Walk With E or anything like that. And I would... a few times I would have a solo, I would, you know, just improvise. Yeah. But as far as the rhythm, and I... at that time I was trying to play just strictly rhythm manjo and I... I just kept it very simple and... I played loud and... and... and straight four four. Yeah. Just a little, little syncopation once in a while. And he never, uh... Once... once in a while, Purnell would... would, uh... try to indicate a chord or, uh... say, uh... you know, quiet, you know, whatever. And George, at that time, he would... sometimes play four or five choruses, just very soft. And the whole band would come way, way down. They had a tremendous dynamic, you know, at that time. Even though the... the band was very robust and driving, once in a while, he was drinking at that time. And when he was feeling real good, he would just keep... and it's real pretty tone, would get very low and just start swinging in the... in the lower register. Yeah. Very plaintive. Okay. Now, um...
